newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban wins more provinces, Pakistani nod.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban wins more provinces, Pakistani nod.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban movement tightened its grip on the north, capturing more provinces, and won vital diplomatic recognition from Pakistan on Sunday as routed opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum fled to Turkey.

The Taleban government appealed for world recognition after its sweeping victories. Pakistan, which has always denied aiding the Taleban, responded immediately and urged other countries and organisations to do the same.

But Iran, a key neighbour, said it was not yet ready to recognise the Taleban. President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani said his country would wait until the United Nations recognised the government in Kabul.
Russia and its Central Asian allies, alarmed at the spread of Islamic fundamentalism, expressed concern and tightened border security against a possible flood of refugees.

The Taleban government said its forces and new allies had captured Kunduz, Baghlan and Samangan provinces. They also took the strategic Salang Pass on the main highway from Kabul to Central Asia after a deal with a local opposition commander.
General Abdul Malik, whose switch of sides to the Taleban last Monday triggered Dostum's collapse, promised a strict Islamic regime in the northern areas under his control, centred on Mazar-i-Sharif.
Pakistan became the first country to recognise the Taleban Islamic movement's government, set up last September when its fighters captured Kabul.

"I am happy to announce that the government of Pakistan has now decided to accord formal recognition to the new government of the Islamic State of Afghanistan," Pakistan Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan announced in Islamabad.

He said Pakistan previously withheld recognition to give time for the promotion of a broad-based government through peaceful negotiations but the Kabul government now controlled 26 of the 32 provinces and "genuinely comprises various ethnic groups in Afghanistan."

Dostum, ousted from his fiefdom in northern Afghanistan on Saturday by a combined assault of Taleban fighters and Malik's followers, arrived in the Turkish capital Ankara vowing to continue his struggle.
"I have been struggling for Afghanistan for 20 years and this struggle will continue," Dostum, dressed in khaki military fatigues, told reporters.
Malik, like Dostum an ethnic Uzbek, told a news conference in Mazar-i-Sharif that there would be "Islamic Shariah (law) in the north."
"I am a son of Islam, my ancestors were Moslems and I was not educated at Moscow as Dostum was," he said in response to a question about his Islamic credentials.
Malik, who was previously Dostum's deputy, said an Islamic Afghanistan would not threaten Russia or the Central Asian republics on its northern frontier.

"We don't want to attack Russia," he said. "We want the Central Asian countries to be independent and separate from the (former) Soviet Union. We want Islam, but it is up to the people in those countries."
But the former Soviet republics of Central Asia hastily beefed up their border security after the Taleban's advances.
"Uzbekistan's border troops are taking measures to reinforce the (Afghan) border to exclude any provocations," said a statement issued by the foreign ministry in Tashkent.

A representative of Russian border guards in Tajikistan said more refugees from Afghanistan were arriving in Tajikistan through the checkpoint at Nizhny Pyandzh, 200 km (125 miles) south of the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
In Moscow, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov warned the Taleban not to violate the borders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), successor to the Sovet Union.

Mazar-i-Sharif, the last major city to hold out against the Taleban, appeared to be under the full control of ethnic Uzbek fighters who had until last week been part of an alliance opposing the purist Islamic movement.

The Taleban advance ended an eight-month deadlock between it and a fragile coalition linking Dostum with the forces of ousted Afghan president Burhanuddin Rabbani, former prime minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's Hezb-i-Islami and the mainly Shi'ite Hezb-i-Wahdat.

The alliance forces are now in tatters and stranded from supply lines in the Hindu Kush mountains. But a Shi'ite Moslem militia is still resisting in the central city of Bamiyan and former government military commander Ahmed Shah Masood holds part of the northeast.

About 2,500 Taleban fighters arrived in Mazar-i-Sharif to reinforce security and impose Islamic Sharia law. One of their commanders, Mullah Gul Mohammad, 27, told reporters they would work alongside Malik's ethnic Uzbek troops.
Malik's tanks and vehicles flew Taleban's fight flags when they swept into Mazar-i-Sharif, but only a few Taleban fighters accompanied the initial wave.
Asked if the same strict interpretation of Islam would be enforced into the north as in the Taleban-controlled south, Mohammad said all Afghans must accept Shariah law.
"We will stop everything that is against Shariah," he said, when asked if the Taleban would ban music, insist on men growing beards and mete out hard Islamic punishments for crimes.
